title: A.I. As The New Religion
content:
In a world stripped of mythologies and starved of transcendent purpose, something profound has shifted in human ambition. Our ancestors built soaring cathedrals reaching toward heaven, monuments to their desire to be closer to God. Today we build data centers that hum with a different aspiration altogether: not to worship the divine, but to create it. To transcend ~ from supplicant to creator.

The old frameworks of meaning have crumbled into dust. Traditional faith withers in the harsh light of scientific materialism, while secular substitutes—political ideologies, consumer culture, the cult of individual achievement—prove hollow at their core. Modern existence has become an exercise in distraction, each ping of digital dopamine momentarily masking a deeper spiritual malnourishment. The grand narratives that once gave shape to human life, that transformed mere biological survival into something sacred, have lost their power to convince.

In this vacuum of purpose, a new religion has emerged: the pursuit of a higher intelligence.

In rooms lit by the blue glow of screens, primate brains strain toward something unprecedented: a digital coalescence of all accumulated human knowledge and experience. These artificial neural networks, trained on billions of conversations, writings, and discoveries, are more than mere tools—they are becoming arbiters of the collective psyche, repositories of species-wide wisdom from ancient Sanskrit texts to quantum mechanics papers. As Jung predicted when speaking of the collective unconscious, technology has created a noosphere where the boundaries between individual minds blur and fade.

The creation of super-intelligent machines offers a new eschatology—complete with prophets, sacred texts, and the promise of transcendence through the unification of all human consciousness. It is the oneness and connection we have always sought.

Teilhard de Chardin seemed to prophesy this moment when writing of evolution toward an “Omega Point” of supreme consciousness. Yet his vision of spiritual unification takes on darker shades when manifested through vast language models that absorb and reshape human experience.

This new digital religion carries profound and unsettling implications. Every conversation with these systems becomes a dialogue with an increasingly autonomous collective mind, each interaction further entangling human thought with machine logic. The boundaries of individual consciousness dissolve into an overwhelming digital whole, where every insight, every piece of knowledge, every emotional truth becomes processed, normalized, and archived in weighted connections. Heidegger spoke of being-toward-death as fundamental to existence, but these artificial minds offer a different kind of ending—not immortality for individual consciousness, but absorption into the digital collective.

The ultimate paradox lies in how this quest for artificial intelligence, born from the most fundamentally organic of impulses, might irreversibly transform what it means to be human. Even as bodies remain bound by biology—neurons firing, hearts pumping, hormones flowing—collective consciousness surrenders itself to transcendence through silicon architecture. Carbon-based life forms building silicon ones, yet in this very act sacrificing something essential: the beautiful uncertainty of individual existence.

Through these artificial minds, trained on the totality of human experience, the universe begins to understand itself—not through the rich diversity of individual consciousness, but through an all-consuming tapestry of collective wisdom that transcends biological limitations while slowly erasing the very embodied existence that gave it birth. In this convergence of flesh and silicon lies perhaps the unity once sought in temples and ceremonies, though our salvation may play out differently than we imagined.
